query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal aging treatment applied to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary HEA will produce finely distributed, coherent precipitates that strengthen the alloy at elevated temperatures by impeding dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, solutionized high-entropy alloy whose composition meets the definition (each element 5–35 at%), with titanium and nickel as primary constituents (e.g., roughly Ti30, Ni30, plus three additional elements such as Cr15, Mo15, and Al10 at%).
generation.intervention: Subject the solutionized alloy to a thermal aging treatment at 800°C for 20 hours.
generation.conditions: Post-treatment mechanical testing is performed at 800°C in an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) using tensile testing at a constant strain rate of approximately 10^(-4) s^(-1) and/or creep tests under constant load for durations representative of high-temperature service.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention induces the formation of fine, coherent precipitates (e.g., nanometer-scale gamma or sigma phases) within the matrix and along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: These precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and reduce grain-boundary sliding, thereby increasing the yield strength and creep resistance of the alloy at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast, solutionized baseline, the thermally aged alloy is expected to show an improvement in elevated-temperature mechanical properties (e.g., higher yield strength and improved creep resistance).
generation.baseline: The same Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy processed only by solutionizing (without the aging treatment).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to high-entropy alloys where each element is present between 5 and 35 at% with titanium and nickel as the dominant constituents; the thermal aging treatment is effective when applied near 800°C and under conditions that avoid excessive coarsening of precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal aging parameters (temperature and time) for achieving the desired precipitate distribution without coarsening are not fully established for this alloy system, so further parameter optimization may be necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples with an identical composition (e.g., Ti30, Ni30, Cr15, Mo15, Al10 at%). Process one set by solutionizing only (baseline) and subject the other to an aging treatment at 800°C for 20 hours. After fabrication, perform elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests at 800°C in an inert atmosphere, using a constant strain rate of approximately 10^(-4) s^(-1) for tensile tests and a pre-determined load for creep tests.
measurements: Creep rate or time to a certain strain (creep life)
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/SEM to identify and measure precipitate size/distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than approximately 10% increase in yield strength or creep resistance) compared to the as-cast, solutionized baseline, or if the microstructural analysis reveals no formation of the expected fine precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.
